summary: FarmShift  is a crop-planning tool built for farmers in The Gambia. Farmers can choose a location or use their current location to view local climate conditions and crop guidance. The app uses NASA POWER rainfall and temperature data to estimate which reviewed crops may fit a location and when to plant. It also provides crop-specific climate checks for a wider set of featured crops, clearly labeling estimated profiles that still need local validation. Additional connected sources include FAO GAEZ crop suitability, ERA5 climate data, satellite vegetation observations, and elevation data. The project addresses the challenge of turning Earth-observation data into practical, location-based information for agricultural planning. By making climate patterns and crop guidance easier to understand, FarmShift  can help farmers explore options, plan rotations, and consider changing conditions—while making clear that its estimates are not yield forecasts or a substitute for local agricultural advice.
details:
FarmShift: Smarter Crop Rotation Through NASA Earth Observation Data

Team METHOD404 | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 | Challenge 07: Field Shift

1. What it does

FarmShift is a decision-support platform that helps farmers choose crops and plan sustainable rotations. Farmers register their farm, enter coordinates and soil details, and the system pulls NASA data (temperature, rainfall, humidity, solar radiation). It compares rotation options against crop characteristics and farmer priorities. A What-If Simulator lets users test scenarios like reduced rainfall or higher temperatures. Rather than recommending a single crop, it shows the long-term benefits and limits of each rotation strategy.

2. Benefits

  • Better-informed farming decisions
  • Sustainable rotations that improve soil health and reduce dependence on one crop
  • Climate adaptation through trend analysis and scenario testing
  • NASA data made accessible to farmers and agricultural professionals
  • Local relevance through soil, location and farmer priorities
  • Comparing rotation options before planting
  • Education on how environment, soil and crops relate

3. Intended impact

The goal is more sustainable, productive and climate-resilient agriculture, starting in The Gambia and possibly expanding. Gambian farmers face unpredictable rainfall, changing temperatures, soil degradation and limited access to useful information. FarmShift aims to bridge the gap between scientific data and practical decisions by:

  • Helping smallholder farmers plant with more confidence
  • Encouraging sustainable rotation
  • Improving understanding of changing conditions
  • Supporting researchers and extension officers
  • Contributing to long-term soil conservation

4. Tools and technologies

Area

Tools

Frontend

React.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet (maps), Recharts (charts)

Backend

Node.js, Express.js (REST APIs)

Database/Auth

Supabase (PostgreSQL + Supabase Auth)

Data processing

Python, NumPy, Pandas

NASA data

POWER (weather, solar), SMAP (soil moisture), GPM (precipitation), MODIS (vegetation, land surface)

Dev/Infra

VS Code / IntelliJ, Git/GitHub, Supabase, Vercel (frontend deployment)

Hardware: standard computers and internet only. No sensors or specialised equipment needed.

5. Creativity and innovation

Most agri apps stop at weather forecasts or single-crop advice. FarmShift plans rotations across multiple seasons. Key innovations:

  • NASA-powered insights: Earth observation data turned into understandable indicators
  • Interactive rotation planning: explore sequences instead of getting one answer
  • What-If simulation: test rainfall and temperature changes
  • Location-aware analysis: farm coordinates linked to relevant datasets
  • Explainable recommendations: shows why an option may suit the farm

It is more than NASA data on a dashboard: it combines environmental data, agricultural knowledge and rotation planning in one experience.

6. Factors considered

  • Accuracy: NASA datasets differ in resolution, method and update frequency, so limitations are shown
  • Local conditions: Gambian crops, soils and smallholder needs
  • Soil health: nutrient needs, nitrogen fixation, conservation
  • Climate variability: scenarios built in
  • Usability: simple interface for all technical levels
  • Security and privacy: authentication and access controls protect farm locations and user data
  • Scalability: architecture can support other regions
  • Scientific responsibility: supports decisions but does not replace professional agronomic advice, and satellite estimates and simulations are kept distinct from real farm measurements
